name: Tara
role: Female Buddha in Vajrayana, female bodhisattva in Mahayana; swift rescuer
summary: Tara is revered as a female Buddha in Vajrayana Buddhism and as a female bodhisattva in Mahayana Buddhism. She rescues beings from danger, and Tibetans honour her as Green Tara and White Tara.
about: In Buddhist tradition Tara, whose name comes from a root meaning 'to cross', helps beings cross over dangers. Vajrayana Buddhists revere her as a female Buddha, while Mahayana Buddhists may see her as a female bodhisattva. Her worship was established at Nalanda by the sixth century, and early images show her beside Avalokiteshvara. A well-known Tibetan story says she was born from a blue lotus that grew in Avalokiteshvara's tears, while another tells of a princess who vowed to always be reborn as a woman. Green Tara is the best-known form, and her praises list twenty-one Taras. Tibetan tradition also holds that Green Tara appeared as the Nepali princess Bhrikuti and White Tara as the Chinese princess Wencheng. Tibetan children often learn her praises.
kidSummary: Tara is a kind and quick-to-help bodhisattva in Tibetan Buddhism. People ask her for help when they are afraid, and green is her colour. Her name means 'one who helps you cross' to safety.

story.title: Tears of compassion
story.text: A Tibetan story says Avalokiteshvara wept when he saw how much suffering there was in the world. Where a tear fell, a blue lotus grew.

story.title: A flower opens
story.text: The lotus opened, and Tara stepped out of it. In many pictures she is green, and she is ready to help right away.

story.title: Always ready to help
story.text: In the praises to her, she is called a swift rescuer. People sing to her about dangers like floods, lions and fear, and she is said to hear them.

story.title: A princess's promise
story.text: Another tale says a princess vowed to keep being reborn as a woman so she could help others, and she is remembered as a form of Tara.

teaches: Fear can be crossed with help and courage
Everyone can become wise and compassionate
emblems: Right hand giving, left hand giving refuge
Mantra Om Tare Tuttare Ture Svaha

family.name: Avalokiteshvara

facts.text: Tara's own pure land is called Arrayed in Turquoise Petals; one teacher says it lies inside Sukhavati, and Amitabha is said to rest on her crown, tying her to his lotus family.
The word tara can also mean 'star' or 'planet', which links her to guiding travellers.
In the 108 Names of Tara she is 'Leader of the caravans', who shows the way to the lost, and Dhruva, the Sanskrit name for the North Star.
White Tara is shown with seven eyes, including eyes on her palms and soles and one on her forehead, and is linked with long life, healing and calm.
Her main form is dark green, a colour said to blend all the others and to stand for awakened activity.
Another story tells of a princess who vowed to be reborn as a woman until all beings are free; the 14th Dalai Lama described this as a feminist movement inside Buddhism.
Tibetan tradition says Green Tara appeared as the Nepali princess Bhrikuti, and White Tara as the Chinese princess Wencheng.
She is often shown as a playful sixteen-year-old girl, in some accounts one who teases self-righteousness.
Tara is also a forest goddess, Khadiravani, 'dweller in the acacia forest', linked with plants, flowers and the wind, which is why she is also known as a healer.
The Manjushrimulakalpa, a text of about the 5th to 8th centuries, calls her the compassion of Avalokiteshvara and the mother of Prince Manjughosha, a name of Manjushri.
Her name comes from a root meaning 'to cross', and her mantra plays on it: tare means 'O Tara', tuttare 'one who helps beings cross', and ture 'swift'.
Tara guards against eight dangers named in her sutra: lions, elephants, fire, snakes, robbers, water, disease and demons; teachers also read them as inner troubles.
A sixth-century carving in Kanheri cave 90 near Mumbai shows an early triad of Avalokiteshvara, Tara and Bhrikuti, one of the oldest known images of her.
A Red Tara practice was said to be hidden as a treasure by Padmasambhava for Yeshe Tsogyal, then found again in the 20th century by the lama Apong Terton.
Tara is really a whole class of forms: ten green, seven white, five yellow, two blue and one red, and a Tibetan painting even shows one with a thousand heads and arms.
Her lotus imagery resembles that of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi, and at least one Tibetan liturgy calls on Lakshmi as Tara.
In Tibetan tradition, Swift Courageous Tara is red, has eight arms and carries a bow and arrow to turn back harmful influences.
Her main mantra, Om Tare Tuttare Ture Svaha, is the same for Buddhists and Hindus alike, though Tibetans say it as 'soha'.
Evidence from Nalanda shows her cult was established by the 6th century, and images of her have turned up in Nepal, Sri Lanka and Indonesia.
Tara is also counted among the ten Mahavidyas in Hindu Shakta tradition, and her fierce Ugra Tara form entered Hindu tantra from Buddhist texts.
In Atisha's 11th-century system each of the 21 Taras has a mantra of her own, for example one for healing and long life and another for wealth.

quiz.q: What does the root of the name Tara mean?
quiz.why: The name comes from a root meaning to cross, as in helping across dangers.

quiz.q: Which colour is Tara most known for?
quiz.why: Green Tara is her main form.

quiz.q: According to a Tibetan story, what did Tara come from?
options: A blue lotus grown from a tear
quiz.why: The story says a blue lotus grew from a tear of Avalokiteshvara.

quiz.q: How many Taras are in the well-known praise?
quiz.why: The Praises to the Twenty-One Taras list twenty-one forms.
